content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Sweet Potatoes, Stage 2 are pre‑cooked sweet‑potato purees designed for infants aged 6–12 months. The puree has a smooth texture, a mild natural sweetness, and is rich in vitamins A and C as well as dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A for eye health.
They have a lower glycemic index than regular potatoes.
Stage 2 purees are typically free of added sugar or salt.
Sweet potatoes are cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions but adapt to temperate climates.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision development, immune function, and healthy skin.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Fiber for digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in sodium
items.content: No added salt makes the product gentle on infants' kidneys.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Sweet‑potato allergy
items.content: Although rare, an allergic reaction is possible; monitor the baby when first introduced.

items.title: Over‑feeding
items.content: Large portions may cause diarrhea due to the high fiber content.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the product refrigerated and use within 3–5 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree warmed, thinning it with breast milk, formula, or water to the desired consistency. You can mix in a small amount of fruit puree for flavor variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator and use within a few days. Discard if the smell or color changes.

corn-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-margari.title: Corn, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Fresh corn cooked with butter or margarine retains its natural sweetness and tender texture. Sautéing gives the kernels a golden crust while the fat adds aroma and enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the oldest cultivated crops, domesticated over 7,000 years ago in Mexico.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, differing in color, size, and flavor.
Yellow corn is rich in carotenoids, which convert to vitamin A during cooking.
Corn is used not only as food but also for biofuel, starch, and animal feed production.
Cooking corn in fat improves the uptake of lutein, an antioxidant present in yellow kernels.

items.title: Rich source of carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides a quick source of energy thanks to its high starch content.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Cooking with butter or margarine enhances the absorption of vitamins A and E found in corn.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn proteins.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or using pre‑seasoned margarine can increase sodium levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be served as a side dish, added to salads, soups, and casseroles. When sautéing in butter or margarine, use a moderate amount of fat and serve immediately to preserve flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh corn in the refrigerator in a plastic bag for up to 3‑5 days. Cooked corn can be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days, or frozen for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat muffins are small, soft cakes made from whole wheat or cracked wheat. They have a moist crumb, a mildly sweet flavor, and a pleasant baked aroma. Wheat muffins are often enjoyed with tea, as a quick breakfast, or as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat muffins can be sweet or savory, depending on added berries, nuts, or spices.
Traditionally baked in muffin tins, they can also be prepared in paper liners for easy serving.
Whole‑grain wheat retains bran and germ, making the muffins more nutritious than those made with refined white flour.
In some cultures they are served with a drizzle of yogurt or honey.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Whole wheat releases glucose slowly, helping maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Wheat muffins provide magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When baked with minimal oil, muffins remain a relatively low‑fat option.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid wheat muffins.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions often contain added sugar, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although not high in fat, a serving can be calorie‑rich due to carbs and add‑ins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy muffins warm or at room temperature, split them and spread low‑fat cottage cheese, yogurt, nut butter, or avocado. They pair well with berries, nuts, seeds, or spices such as cinnamon and vanilla.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Reheat before eating in the oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit topping (5039) is a blend of dried and/or fresh fruits designed to be added to desserts, yogurts, cereals, and drinks. The fruits retain their characteristic aroma, sweetness, and nutrients, providing a bright flavor and vivid color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix may include pineapple, mango, kiwi, strawberry, blueberry and other exotic fruits.
Dried fruits in the topping keep most of their vitamins, especially vitamin C and carotenoids.
Fruit topping is often used in vegan and gluten‑free recipes as a natural sweetener.
Sugar content varies depending on the fruit types and processing level.
Traditionally, fruit topping is served in Asian cuisine, for example in sticky‑rice desserts.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fruits provide vitamin C, vitamin A, folate and other antioxidants that support immunity and skin health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike nut toppings, fruit topping contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in fruits encourage the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Natural sweetness
items.content: The natural sugars in fruits allow reduction of added sugar in recipes.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific fruits included in the topping.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High natural sugar levels can be an issue for people with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If fruits are not thoroughly washed, pesticide residues may remain.

items.title: Dried fruit glucose concentration
items.content: Dried fruits have a more concentrated glucose level, which can raise blood sugar quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit topping can be mixed into yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, ice cream, baked goods, or used as a garnish for desserts. For extra aroma, fruits can be lightly toasted in a pan or oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the topping in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Dried fruits keep up to 6 months, fresh fruits up to 5 days in the refrigerator. Discard if mold or off‑odors appear.
